title: Fourteen Floors Down
part: PART ONE: TWO WAYS OF KNOWING

pages.text:
*Jun's phone says: 32 degrees, sunny, arrival 2:10. Nari's river says: not yet.*

On the fourteenth floor of a tall grey building in Seoul, Jun had lived for twelve years without once being asked to carry anything heavier than a backpack, and now his mother was zipping a suitcase the size of a small refrigerator.

"Three weeks," she said. "Your grandparents' house. Clean air. Ice-cold watermelon."

"I have hagwon," said Jun. Hagwon was the name for the classes he went to every afternoon after school, and he was good at them.

"Hagwon is closed for the summer break," said his mother, "and I checked."

She had checked. That was the trouble with his mother, who checked everything twice and then a third time for luck. Jun pushed his round glasses up his nose and looked around his room for a way out. There was none. The suitcase sat on the floor like a very large, very calm dog.
pages.image: In a tidy modern apartment bedroom on a high floor with a big window showing city towers, Jun, a thin 12-year-old boy in round black-framed glasses and a white T-shirt with a small robot picture, stares in dismay at an enormous open suitcase on the floor while Jun's mother, a slim woman with short wavy dark-brown hair in a neat bob wearing a pale blue blouse, kneels and zips it.

pages.text:
He packed his own bag of important things, since nobody could be trusted with it. Charger. Backup charger. Notebook. Vacation homework, in a plastic folder. A jar of his mother's kimchi, which she had wrapped in three plastic bags and told him to hold upright like a baby.

"Be nice to your cousin," said his father on the phone, from the office where he was going to be until late, as usual. "Nari is a good kid."

"I'm always nice," said Jun.

There was a small silence on the line. Jun had the feeling that somebody, somewhere, had almost laughed.

At the bus terminal his mother pressed a bag of cut pear into his hands, kissed the top of his head and said, "Call me every night." He promised. Then he climbed onto the bus in his brand-new white sneakers, found a window seat, and watched the concrete world slide away.
pages.image: At a busy city bus terminal, Jun, a thin 12-year-old boy in round black-framed glasses, a white T-shirt with a small robot picture, light grey shorts and bright white sneakers with a black crossbody phone pouch, holds a jar wrapped in plastic bags and a bag of cut pear beside a big rolling suitcase, while Jun's mother, a slim woman with short wavy dark-brown hair in a neat bob wearing a pale blue blouse, kisses the top of his head.

pages.text:
For the first hour there were buildings, then smaller buildings, then a factory, then a field. Then, suddenly, there was nothing but green.

Rice paddies lay in the valleys like bright wet mirrors. Hills stood in rows, each a little paler than the last, and a river shone far below the road. Jun watched all of it out of the corner of his eye, because his real attention was on his phone.

Four bars. Then three. Then two. He checked the weather, which said sunny, ten percent chance of rain. He checked the map, which said he was doing very well. When the bus went through a long tunnel, he came out the other side with one bar, and a small, cold feeling he did not have a name for.

He had never been anywhere he could not search for. He held the phone a little tighter, like a railing, and told himself that three weeks was only twenty-one days, which was only five hundred and four hours, which was only a lot.
pages.image: Jun, a thin 12-year-old boy in round black-framed glasses and a white T-shirt, sits by the window of a moving intercity bus looking down at the phone in his hand with a worried face, while outside the window bright green rice paddies, rows of hills and a shining river glide past.

pages.text:
The bus dropped him at a rusty shelter on a dusty road in the middle of a hot afternoon. Then it drove away with a wheeze, and the silence it left behind was not silence at all. Cicadas screamed from every tree, so loud that Jun's teeth hummed.

There were no grandparents. There was no taxi, no station, not even a sign. There was a bench, a road going two ways, and a lot of sky.

Jun checked his phone. Two-oh-six, it said. Four minutes early, which was exactly how he liked to be. He had a plan for this part: grandparents, hugs, watermelon. He stood very straight, in case someone was watching, and pulled his suitcase upright by the handle. One of its little wheels fell off.

Then he noticed the wheelbarrow. It sat under a tree, green and dented and splashed with mud, and behind it, half hidden by the shade, stood a girl with a long braid and a straw hat hanging down her back by a string.
pages.image: At a rusty bus shelter on a dusty country road in bright afternoon heat, Jun, a thin 12-year-old boy in round black-framed glasses, a white T-shirt and white sneakers with a black phone pouch, stands stiffly beside a big suitcase, while under a leafy tree nearby a dented green wheelbarrow sits and Nari, a sunburnt girl in a faded sunflower-yellow T-shirt with a long black braid and a straw hat hanging on her back, watches him.

pages.text:
The girl looked at his suitcase. She looked at his sneakers. She looked at the phone in his hand, and then, for rather a long time, at his face.

"You're four minutes late," she said.

"The bus was early," said Jun. "I'm four minutes early. Your clock is wrong."

"I don't have a clock." She squinted at the sky and sniffed the air like a dog. "You're late. And you brought all that?"

Jun opened his mouth to explain about the bus schedule, and the wheel, and the difference between early and late. But the girl had already picked up his suitcase, which he had needed both arms to lift, and dropped it into the wheelbarrow as if it were a bag of feathers.

"I'm Nari," she said, in the voice of someone who has already made up her mind about you. "Try to keep up."

Then she set off down the road, pushing his entire suitcase in a wheelbarrow, and did not look back once to see if he was coming.
pages.image: Nari, a strong sunburnt eleven-year-old girl with one thick long black braid tied with a red rubber band, a faded sunflower-yellow T-shirt and a straw hat on her back, lifts Jun's big suitcase into a dented green wheelbarrow with a cheeky look while Jun, a thin boy in round black-framed glasses and a white T-shirt with white sneakers, gapes at her beside a rusty bus shelter.
